questions.question: For $A^{(1)}=\begin{pmatrix}4&3\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, perform one QR iteration using a Givens rotation that zeros the $\left(2,1\right)$ entry. Give $r$, $\cos\theta$, $\sin\theta$, and $A^{(2)}=R^{(1)}Q^{(1)}$ to $4$ decimal places.
Given $A^{(1)}=\begin{pmatrix}5&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix}$, compute one QR iteration by first forming a Givens QR factorization. Estimate the eigenvalues from the diagonal of the resulting $A^{(2)}$.
questions.expected: Use $r=\sqrt{5^2+2^2}=\sqrt{29}=5.3852$, $\cos\theta=5/\sqrt{29}=0.9285$, and $\sin\theta=2/\sqrt{29}=0.3714$. Then $R^{(1)}=GA^{(1)}\approx\begin{pmatrix}5.3852&2.5997\\0&1.1142\end{pmatrix}$ and $A^{(2)}=R^{(1)}G^T\approx\begin{pmatrix}5.9655&0.4140\\0.4140&1.0345\end{pmatrix}$. The QR estimate is $\lambda_1\approx5.9655$ and $\lambda_2\approx1.0345$.

questions.question: For $A^{(2)}=\begin{pmatrix}6.2265&0.2209\\0.2205&1.7748\end{pmatrix}$, use the diagonal QR rule to estimate the eigenvalues, then check the estimate using the trace and determinant of the original matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}5&2\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$.
questions.expected: The QR estimate reads the diagonal after near convergence: $\lambda_1\approx6.2265$ and $\lambda_2\approx1.7748$. Check $\lambda_1+\lambda_2\approx6.2265+1.7748=8.0013\approx\operatorname{tr}(A)=8$, and $\lambda_1\lambda_2\approx6.2265\cdot1.7748=11.0526\approx\det(A)=5\cdot3-2\cdot2=11$.

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$, compute the exact eigenvalues using $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$.

Apply one power-method iteration to $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$ starting from $x^{(0)}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$. Normalize using the infinity norm and estimate the dominant eigenvalue using the component ratio formula.
questions.expected: Compute $y^{(0)}=Ax^{(0)}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\end{pmatrix}$. With $\lVert y^{(0)}\rVert_\infty=4$, $x^{(1)}=y^{(0)}/\lVert y^{(0)}\rVert_\infty=\begin{pmatrix}0.75\\1\end{pmatrix}$. The ratio estimate from the second component is $\lambda\approx y^{(0)}_2/x^{(0)}_2=4/1=4$; the formula used is $y^{(n)}=Ax^{(n)}$, $x^{(n+1)}=y^{(n)}/\lVert y^{(n)}\rVert$.

questions.question: Use one shifted inverse-power setup step for $A=\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ with shift $\mu=1.8$ and starting vector $x^{(0)}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$. Solve $(A-\mu I)y=x^{(0)}$ and normalize $y$ by the infinity norm.
questions.expected: First form $A-\mu I=\begin{pmatrix}2.2&1\\1&0.2\end{pmatrix}$. Solve $\begin{pmatrix}2.2&1\\1&0.2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}y_1\\y_2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$, giving $y_1=-0.8$ and $y_2=9$. Since $\lVert y\rVert_\infty=9$, the normalized vector is $x^{(1)}=\begin{pmatrix}-0.0889\\1\end{pmatrix}$. The method applies the power method to $(A-\mu I)^{-1}$ to target the eigenvalue closest to $\mu$.

questions.question: For the system $Ax=b$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$ and $b=\begin{pmatrix}1\\5\end{pmatrix}$, perform one Jacobi iteration from $x^{(0)}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix}$.
questions.expected: Jacobi uses $x_i^{(n+1)}=\left(b_i-\sum_{j\neq i}a_{ij}x_j^{(n)}\right)/a_{ii}$. Thus $x_1^{(1)}=(1-1\cdot0)/4=0.25$ and $x_2^{(1)}=(5-2\cdot0)/3=1.6667$, so $x^{(1)}=\begin{pmatrix}0.25\\1.6667\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$ and $b=\begin{pmatrix}1\\5\end{pmatrix}$, perform one Gauss-Seidel iteration from $x^{(0)}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix}$.
questions.expected: Gauss-Seidel uses updated components immediately. First $x_1^{(1)}=(1-1\cdot0)/4=0.25$; then $x_2^{(1)}=(5-2x_1^{(1)})/3=(5-0.5)/3=1.5$. Therefore $x^{(1)}=\begin{pmatrix}0.25\\1.5\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$, suppose $K(A)=3.5$, $\lVert b-A\tilde{x}\rVert=0.02$, and $\lVert b\rVert=4$. Use the conditioning bound to estimate the maximum possible relative error $\lVert x-\tilde{x}\rVert/\lVert x\rVert$.
questions.expected: Use $\frac{\lVert x-\tilde{x}\rVert}{\lVert x\rVert}\leq K(A)\frac{\lVert b-A\tilde{x}\rVert}{\lVert b\rVert}$. Substitution gives $\frac{\lVert x-\tilde{x}\rVert}{\lVert x\rVert}\leq3.5\cdot\frac{0.02}{4}=0.0175$, so the relative error is bounded by $1.75\%$.

questions.question: Given $P=I$, $L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$, $U=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\0&4\end{pmatrix}$, and $b=\begin{pmatrix}5\\10\end{pmatrix}$, solve $Ax=b$ using $PA=LU$.
questions.expected: First solve $Ly=Pb=b$: $y_1=5$ and $2y_1+y_2=10$, so $y_2=0$. Then solve $Ux=y$: $4x_2=0$, so $x_2=0$, and $3x_1+x_2=5$, so $x_1=5/3=1.6667$. Therefore $x=\begin{pmatrix}1.6667\\0\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.question: Explain why QR iteration preserves the eigenvalues of the original matrix at every step.
questions.expected: If $A^{(k)}=Q^{(k)}R^{(k)}$, then $A^{(k+1)}=R^{(k)}Q^{(k)}=(Q^{(k)})^TA^{(k)}Q^{(k)}$. Because $Q^{(k)}$ is orthogonal, this is an orthogonal similarity transformation. Similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial and hence the same eigenvalues.

questions.question: In a QR eigenvalue computation, when is it reasonable to read the eigenvalues from the diagonal of $A^{(k)}$, and what warning sign says the estimate is still unreliable?
questions.expected: It is reasonable when $A^{(k)}$ is close to triangular, meaning the entries below the diagonal are approximately $0$. The diagonal entries then approximate the eigenvalues. If the off-diagonal entries are still large compared with the diagonal scale, the iteration has not converged and the diagonal entries may be poor eigenvalue estimates.

questions.question: State the practical difference between QR factorization and QR iteration.
questions.expected: QR factorization is one decomposition $A=QR$, where $Q$ is orthogonal and $R$ is upper triangular. QR iteration repeatedly factorizes $A^{(k)}=Q^{(k)}R^{(k)}$ and then forms $A^{(k+1)}=R^{(k)}Q^{(k)}$ to drive the matrix toward triangular form so that eigenvalues can be read from the diagonal.

questions.question: Why is computing eigenvalues from the characteristic polynomial usually avoided for large matrices, even though it works for a small $2\times2$ matrix?
questions.expected: For large matrices, forming and solving the characteristic polynomial can be numerically unstable and computationally expensive. Small perturbations in polynomial coefficients may cause large changes in roots. Iterative methods such as QR iteration work with stable orthogonal transformations and are therefore preferred.

questions.question: Which statement best describes why a large condition number $K(A)$ matters when solving $Ax=b$?
options: A large $K(A)$ means small residual or data errors can produce large relative errors in $x$.
A large $K(A)$ guarantees that Jacobi iteration converges in one step.
A large $K(A)$ means $A$ has only positive eigenvalues.
A large $K(A)$ means $A^{-1}$ does not exist.
questions.expected: The correct answer is: A large $K(A)$ means small residual or data errors can produce large relative errors in $x$. The bound $\frac{\lVert x-\tilde{x}\rVert}{\lVert x\rVert}\leq K(A)\frac{\lVert b-A\tilde{x}\rVert}{\lVert b\rVert}$ shows this sensitivity directly.

questions.question: Which method is most directly designed to approximate the eigenvalue of $A$ with largest magnitude?
questions.expected: The correct answer is: Power method. It repeatedly computes $y^{(n)}=Ax^{(n)}$ and normalizes, so the component in the dominant eigenvector direction tends to dominate when the required assumptions hold.
